cells.tense: The grip has already opened and the finished thing is free to go.
cells.act: give it what it needs today, not what it is scheduled for
cells.ask: Pick something finished. Notice what it actually needs right now — water, a last sentence, a goodbye — and do that, then leave whatever comes next alone.
cells.core:
The door isn't something you push on. When something has run its course, your hands open around it, and what's left is a clean space you didn't have to fight for. You don't need an ending to prove anything happened. The finished thing leaves; you stay whole.

What hasn't finished yet is a different job. Something near you wants looking after and can't be hurried, and you can give it today's attention without deciding how it should come out. Then step back. Your release isn't only for endings — it's also how you carry what's still small, in the same open hands, without needing it to be done.
cells.sheetLine: You can let go without having to lose anything.

cells.tense: The leaving is being done before the thing has finished growing.
cells.act: do the plain version first, before the plans
cells.ask: Before any plans today, do the plain version of a practice you already have — then sit beside one unfinished thing for an hour without touching it.
cells.core:
Where something's growing, you've started leaving early. Giving it up ahead of time looks like strength, and it keeps you ahead of a verdict you'd rather not sit for. But you take your hands off before the thing has had its day, and what you call surrender looks, up close, like not being there at the end.

Staying is what teaches the difference. A small practice, repeated today, plain and unglamorous, puts your hands back on something real and shows them the gap between releasing a thing and dropping it. Sit with one unfinished piece and conclude nothing about it. Release is supposed to come after completion, not instead of it.
cells.sheetLine: You're letting go before there's something to let go of.

cells.tense: The grip is still closed on what finished a long time ago.
cells.act: carry it without tightening around it
cells.ask: Carry what you're still holding for one hour without squeezing it — no fixing, no last call. Then put the hour down and see what's different.
cells.core:
What's finished is still in your hands. You turn it over, keep it ready, hold it so nothing moves except through you. Standing guard like that takes everything, and it's the only pace you've got, so nothing else gets to land.

Your shoulders can outlast this, though. For one hour, carry what's still unfinished without squeezing it. And when someone asks you to shrink what you've done or what you need, hold your shape instead. That kind of holding is a grip too, but it ends by letting go from strength rather than from empty, and the strength is what you already have.
cells.sheetLine: Your hands are tired from holding what's already over.

cells.tense: The release is happening while your hands say they are still holding on.
cells.act: tend it small and ask nothing of it
cells.ask: Put something finished where you'll see it for a few days without deciding anything. Each morning, tend one thing that's still small — water it, feed it — and ask nothing of it.
cells.core:
Some letting go doesn't feel like letting go. Something gets set down and its shape stays in your grip, and the account you give is that you're still holding on. The hands are doing one thing and the story is doing another. From the inside it's hard to say which is true.

Try it the other way: leave something finished in view, with no decision about whether it's over. And put your hands on something still growing — just today's care for it, no result required. You don't have to settle what happened. Watch your hands around the small living thing and take that as the answer.
cells.sheetLine: You've put it down and your hands haven't heard yet.
